claims.text: The initial material is a homogeneous, single-phase, disordered FCC high-entropy alloy.
Intermediate-temperature annealing at 400–800°C can induce intragranular nanoscale ordering and intermetallic precipitation in the initially single-phase alloy.
The annealing-induced precipitates may be ordered L12 or κ-type phases dispersed within an FCC matrix.
The ordered precipitates pin dislocation slip segments.
The ordered precipitates suppress alternative deformation pathways such as multiple slip and twinning.
Suppression of dislocation motion and alternative deformation pathways lowers strain-hardening capacity.
Lower strain-hardening capacity increases strain localization and stress concentration.
Strain localization and stress concentration promote premature crack nucleation and brittle failure.
Long-range ordered phases in many high- and medium-entropy alloys are intrinsically brittle and exhibit poor ductility.
Single-phase FCC high- and medium-entropy alloys can exhibit a rapid decrease in ductility at intermediate temperatures of 400–800°C.
Conventional-alloy intermediate-temperature ductility loss may be controlled by grain-boundary weakening caused by impurity segregation.
The baseline homogeneous FCC alloy has favorable strength and ductility because multiple deformation mechanisms operate in the absence of ordered precipitates.
Relative to the homogenized baseline, the annealed alloy will have lower ductility.
Relative to the homogenized baseline, the annealed alloy will have lower strain-hardening capability.
The annealed alloy will exhibit cleavage facets or intergranular fracture signatures indicative of brittle failure.

The proposed comparison uses the same alloy composition in homogenized and intermediate-temperature-annealed conditions, followed by room-temperature tensile testing and microstructural characterization.
The proposed embrittlement mechanism may not apply at extremely high or cryogenic test temperatures, or when annealing does not produce significant ordering.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis distinguishes an intragranular ordering mechanism from conventional grain-boundary-controlled embrittlement, but the predicted outcome accepts intergranular fracture as evidence for the proposed intragranular mechanism. Intergranular fracture would instead be compatible with the conventional grain-boundary explanation.

The experiment requires annealing that induces ordering, but the rule treats failure to form ordered precipitates as falsification of the causal hypothesis. That result would show failure of the intervention or annealing conditions rather than decisively refute the effect of precipitates once formed.
